title: Name the mechanism: SN1, SN2, E1 or E2
asks: A reaction and its conditions are given. Say which mechanism operates and which species acts as the base or nucleophile.

know.h: {{SN2}} is one step: the nucleophile attacks the back of the carbon as the leaving group leaves. Rate = k[nucleophile][substrate], no intermediate, inversion.
{{SN1}} is stepwise: the leaving group leaves first to give a carbocation (the slow step), then a nucleophile adds. Rate = k[substrate] only.
{{E1}} starts from the same carbocation as {{SN1}}: a weak base, usually the solvent, removes a hydrogen from the carbon next to the positive carbon and the alkene forms.
{{E2}} is one step: a strong base removes a hydrogen from the carbon next to the leaving group while the leaving group leaves. Rate = k[substrate][base].

Classify the carbon that carries the leaving group. {{SN2}}: methyl > primary > secondary, and tertiary does not react. {{SN1}} and {{E1}}: tertiary > secondary, and primary and methyl never react this way because their carbocations are too unstable.

Strong bases have conjugate acids with {{pKa}} near 16 or above: {{HO-}} (15.7), {{CH3O-}} (15.5), {{CH3CH2O-}} (15.9), {{(CH3)3CO-}} (17) and hydride from NaH. A strong base makes the reaction bimolecular: {{E2}}, or {{SN2}} on a methyl or primary carbon.
know.from: pKa table; flowchart; FA24 Exam 2, Q2B

know.h: tert-Butoxide is a strong base and a poor nucleophile because it is bulky. It gives {{E2}} even with a primary halide. On a methyl halide it can only do {{SN2}}, because there is no hydrogen to remove.
know.from: Lecture 11/05, p. 3; flowchart; FA24 Exam 2, Q5A

know.h: Weak bases that are good nucleophiles attack carbon instead of removing a hydrogen: {{HS-}} (126,000 in the lecture table, {{pKa}} of {{H2S}} 10), {{I-}} (80,000), {{N3-}} (8,000), cyanide, and acetate (630, {{pKa}} of the acid 4). They give {{SN2}} on methyl, primary and secondary carbons.

Neutral water and alcohols are poor nucleophiles (relative rate 1) and weak bases. With a tertiary or secondary substrate they wait for the carbocation: the solvent is then the nucleophile ({{SN1}}) or the base ({{E1}}). There is no hydroxide or alkoxide in the flask unless it was added.
Solvents. Polar protic solvents are hydrogen-bond donors (water, methanol, ethanol, acetic acid) and favor {{SN1}} and {{E1}}. Polar aprotic solvents (DMSO, DMF, acetone, acetonitrile) favor {{SN2}}.

The flowchart. Methyl: {{SN2}}. Primary: {{SN2}}, except {{E2}} with a bulky strong base. Secondary: strong base gives {{E2}}; a weak base that is a fair nucleophile in a polar aprotic solvent gives {{SN2}}; a weak base and poor nucleophile in a polar protic solvent gives {{SN1}} and {{E1}}. Tertiary: strong base gives {{E2}}; otherwise {{SN1}} and {{E1}}.
Heat favors elimination. tert-Butyl bromide in water gives the alcohol by {{SN1}} at lower temperature and more alkene by {{E1}} at high temperature, from the same carbocation.
A leaving group on a double-bond carbon (vinyl) does neither {{SN1}} nor {{SN2}}. An allyl substrate does both.
Skill: read the role from the product. A species that ends up bonded to the carbon acted as the nucleophile. A species that ends up carrying one more hydrogen, next to a new C=C, acted as the base.

method: Find the leaving group and classify its carbon: methyl, primary, secondary or tertiary (and check that the carbon is not part of a double bond).
Name the reagent: a strong base (small or bulky), a weak base that is a good nucleophile, or nothing but a neutral solvent.
Name the solvent: polar protic or polar aprotic. It matters most for a secondary carbon.

Walk the flowchart: a strong base means a bimolecular reaction ({{E2}}, or {{SN2}} on methyl and unhindered primary); a neutral solvent alone on a tertiary or secondary carbon means a carbocation ({{SN1}} and {{E1}}).
Look at the product asked about and the temperature: a substitution product comes from {{SN1}} or {{SN2}}, an alkene from {{E1}} or {{E2}}, and heat raises the share of elimination.
State the role of each species: the one that bonds to carbon is the nucleophile, the one that takes the hydrogen is the base, and it must be a species that is really in the flask.

pitfalls.h: Writing hydroxide or an alkoxide as the base when the flask holds only water or an alcohol. In a solvolysis the neutral solvent is the base or the nucleophile.
Calling an elimination {{E2}} when there is no strong base. With only a weak base the alkene comes from the carbocation: {{E1}}.
Choosing {{SN1}} for a tertiary halide in water when NaOH has been added. A strong base gives {{E2}}, and the alcohol is not formed.
Choosing {{SN1}} or {{E1}} for a primary or methyl halide because the solvent is protic. Those carbocations never form.
Treating tert-butoxide as a nucleophile on a primary halide, or expecting it to eliminate a methyl halide that has no hydrogen on a neighbouring carbon.
Sending a good nucleophile that is a weak base ({{HS-}}, {{N3-}}, acetate) down the {{E2}} path just because it has a negative charge.
